analysis.one_liner: Mandated approval of the Keystone XL pipeline permit, cutting off further federal environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in four House committees and died at the end of the 112th Congress, with not a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill ordered the President, within 60 days, to grant the cross-border permit for the Keystone XL pipeline that would carry Canadian oil sands crude to Gulf Coast refineries. If the President did not act, the permit would go into effect automatically, by operation of law. It also declared the 2011 environmental review complete, stating that no further federal environmental review would be required, while allowing a limited reconsideration of the route through Nebraska.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada, the company seeking to build the pipeline, would get its permit without further review. Canadian oil sands producers would gain a guaranteed route to U.S. Gulf Coast markets, and Gulf Coast refiners would gain access to heavy Canadian crude. Construction workers would get temporary pipeline jobs; the bill's own findings claim 20,000 direct jobs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the President to grant the permit for the September 2008 Keystone XL application within 60 days of enactment, unless the President formally determines the pipeline does not serve the national interest and reports a justification to Congress [S2][S3].
If the President makes no determination and takes no action in 60 days, the permit goes into effect by operation of law — meaning inaction counts as approval [S2][S3].
The permit would be issued under conditions tied to TransCanada's construction, mitigation, and safety plans from the 2011 environmental impact statement [S3].

The bill's findings argue the pipeline improves energy security by replacing imports from less stable suppliers, creates 20,000 direct jobs, and increases Keystone system capacity by 700,000 barrels per day [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the environmental risk: the bill declares the 2011 environmental impact statement complete and says no further federal environmental review would be required, even before the Nebraska route was settled [S3]. Landowners and communities along the route — including areas where the line could still cross Nebraska's Sand Hills region — would bear the spill risk. Citizens lose the ordinary role of an executive permit decision in their own review process.

drawbacks.text: The bill states that the August 2011 final environmental impact statement satisfies all requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act and that 'no further Federal environmental review shall be required,' cutting the review short even though the Nebraska route was still unresolved at the time [S3].

The default rule counts presidential inaction as approval: if the President neither grants the permit nor formally determines it is not in the national interest within 60 days, the permit takes effect by operation of law [S2][S3].
Even the Nebraska reconsideration is hedged: if the President does not approve the governor's route within 10 days of submission, it is considered approved by operation of law [S3].

The job gains are construction-phase and temporary; the bill's own findings cite 20,000 direct jobs, but a pipeline build does not produce a permanent workforce, so the lasting employment benefit is small relative to the permanent change in the landscape and risk profile [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — temporary construction work and a new oil supply line — flow mostly to a single company and to oil sands producers and refiners, while its most distinctive provisions work to shut the door on further environmental review and to turn presidential inaction into approval. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the Nebraska routing question was still open when the bill demanded a decision, and that mandating the outcome removed the normal chance for affected communities and agencies to finish their review.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in four House committees and their subcommittees after referral in December 2011 and never came to a vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Denny Rehberg (R-MT) introduced the bill on December 1, 2011; no other House member signed on as a cosponsor [S1][S4].
It was referred to four committees — Transportation and Infrastructure, Foreign Affairs, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources — and then to subcommittees in early December 2011 [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote occurred, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1][S5].

The bill directed the President to grant the Keystone XL permit within 60 days, with the permit going into effect by operation of law if the President took no action, and barred any further federal environmental review beyond the 2011 statement [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the President retained discretion over the Keystone XL permit and the environmental review process was not short-circuited by statute. TransCanada and Canadian oil sands producers did not get the automatic permit this bill promised, while route-area landowners and pipeline opponents kept the opportunity for further review.

for.name: Rep. Denny Rehberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 1, 2011 to force approval of the Keystone XL permit [S1][S3].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Foreign Affairs, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Natural Resources Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in December 2011 and never reported the bill back to the House for a vote [S5].

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed legislation setting an artificial deadline for the Keystone XL permit decision.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred; the sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors [S4], while the Democratic President opposed mandating the permit on a deadline.

industries.note: The bill would have handed the company its permit by default within 60 days and barred further federal environmental review, removing the normal process for the communities and agencies weighing the project [S3]. The public would absorb the spill and routing risk the review was meant to resolve.

A guaranteed pipeline to Gulf Coast markets would lock in a route for oil sands crude that might otherwise go by rail to Asia or the U.S. coast; the bill's findings frame this as displacing imports from less stable suppliers [S3]. The benefit accrues to producers, not to consumers, who see little direct price relief from a single pipeline.

Refiners along the Gulf would gain a steady supply of heavy Canadian crude to process, which supports refinery jobs. Whether savings pass to consumers at the pump is debated, so the public benefit is indirect at best.

Mandating the pipeline would displace crude currently moved by rail and truck, costing those transport businesses revenue. Their loss in this case runs alongside the public interest in less spill-prone transport, though both positions here are indirect.
